t: Random Pick Index — Hash Map vs. Reservoir Sampling
o: We must return a uniformly random index among all positions where `nums[i] == target`. The constructor gets the whole array once, then `pick` may be called many times. In the example, `pick(3)` on `[1,2,3,3,3]` must return 2, 3, or 4 each with probability 1/3, while `pick(1)` has only one candidate (index 0). Constraints are small (n ≤ 2·10⁴, ≤10⁴ calls), so both precomputation with hash maps and per-call streaming work comfortably; the interesting trade-off is memory vs. pick-time.
k: Precompute target → list of indices once, then answer each pick in O(1) via uniform random choice.
Reservoir sampling lets you answer picks without any extra storage: scan the array, keep the i-th match with probability 1/i.
Uniformity proof for reservoir sampling: after k matches, each earlier match survives with probability ∏(j/(j+1)) = 1/k.

a.i: During construction, group all indices by their value. Then `pick(target)` is just picking a uniformly random element from the precomputed list of indices for that target. This gives O(1) picks at the cost of O(n) extra memory, which is ideal when `pick` is called many times.
s: In the constructor, build a dictionary mapping each distinct value to the list of its indices.
In `pick`, fetch the list for `target` and return a uniformly random index from it using randint / randInt / random index selection.
a.t: O(n) preprocessing; O(1) per pick — building the map dominates construction, lookups and random choice are constant time.
a.sp: O(n) — every index is stored exactly once across all map values.

a.i: Scan the array counting occurrences of `target`; keep the current best answer. When we see the k-th occurrence, replace the stored answer with it with probability 1/k. By induction, after processing everything, each of the k occurrences was last chosen with probability 1/k, giving perfect uniformity while storing only one index.
s: Iterate over nums; whenever nums[i] == target, increment count.
With probability 1/count, set result = i (e.g., if rand() % count == 0).
a.t: O(n) per pick — a full scan of the array is required for each call.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only a counter and the current answer are kept.

w: Prefer the hash-map approach when memory is fine and picks are frequent (O(1) per query); prefer reservoir sampling when memory is constrained or the data arrives as a stream you cannot store — this is the classic follow-up ('what if the array is huge / streaming?'). Pitfalls: forgetting to seed-free use of rand (rand() % count is fine since count ≥ 1 inside the branch), off-by-one in sampling probability (use randInt(1, count) == 1 or rand() % count == 0), and assuming target always exists (guaranteed here, but defensive code should handle empty candidate lists). Edge cases: single-element arrays, targets appearing exactly once, and many repeated calls for the same target.
